prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B035 as my single-part configuration with Katori and Ye, and I have not changed it since round 1. Having read the full exchange, the scientific case rests on a specific physical step that the chair asked us to name. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal makes the clock transition insensitive to the trapping light, so that thousands of neutral atoms can be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime and interrogated in parallel. That is what turns a single-ion clock into a statistical one and what opened the 10^-18 regime, which Ye's group then reached by controlling density-dependent and many-body shifts and by pushing laser coherence. This is neither the comb (a counting mechanism) nor ion control (a single quantum system), so I regard it as a distinct invention and not a refinement. The result is reproduced at JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE and NIST, and it already yields a gravitational redshift resolved across a millimetre-scale sample, which is a clue from nature that matters to someone who works on gravity. The case is mature: the interpretation is stable and recognition is neither premature nor a lifetime award. I do not think the pending redefinition of the second is necessary; it is a supporting consequence. On attribution, all eight of us propose the same two names, which tells us the concept-plus-realization split fits the record. I propose a citation that names the invention and its realization and the 10^-18 level, without claiming every clock result.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains scope and precedent: the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize cover much of the enabling toolkit, and a sceptic can read lattice clocks as an excellent refinement of recognised metrology. It is also a precision-measurement achievement and not the discovery of a new phenomenon, and I still think B006 and B008 are arguably higher in pure scientific significance. The two-name credit leaves out Lemonde, Takamoto, Lisdat, the Yb groups and the ion-clock community, and no citation wording fully repairs that. Finally, the redefinition of the second is undecided, and some colleagues (Johansson, Kroll, Olsson) would prefer to see it settled first. I do not agree that this should delay a prize, but I accept it is a legitimate difference of judgment and not an error.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B008 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as the clearest package of theory, quick decisive experiment and field-wide consequence, but says he would not defend it against a well-argued shift to B035 because of the credit problem.
responses.response: I agree with your description of the science and I ranked B008 second in my opening ballot, so I am not dismissing it. Our shared difficulty is the one you name: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe route that Molenkamp measured, Zhang is deceased, and the three-dimensional generalisation by Fu, Kane and Mele, Moore and Balents and Hasan lies outside the credit set. I also see more overlap with the 2016 prize than you do, since the idea that topology organises electronic matter was recognised then, even if the Z2 time-reversal case was not. A three-name citation that has to carve around these omissions would be harder to defend than a two-name clock prize. I therefore keep B008 as my first alternative, and I would support it later if the committee can settle the HgTe credit. Your acknowledgement that B035 is the cleaner proposal on credit is the point on which we now agree.

responses.point: Pearce keeps B035 and adds B023 for Halzen alone, as a second part crediting conception and leadership of IceCube and the discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, while admitting that one name for Halzen is an attribution compromise.
responses.response: I appreciate that you flagged the compromise and your proximity through Fermi-LAT yourself. My view of IceCube has not moved. A diffuse flux is established, but the origin of most of it is unresolved, source identification at TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 is still at modest significance, and independent confirmation from KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD is incomplete. A prize needs a settled interpretation, and here the central question of what produces these neutrinos is still open. The credit is the second problem: with only one seat left beside Katori and Ye, naming Halzen alone puts Karle and Spiering outside, and I would not select among them in a collaboration-scale case. Adding a part that cannot be credited cleanly would weaken a prize whose first part is strong, so I do not support B023 as a second part this year. It remains a good candidate for a later year if source identification firms up.

responses.point: Johansson moved to B035 first and treats the opening breadth of support as a signal to be tested and not as merit. He notes the case would be stronger if the second were already redefined and that ion-clock and other Sr and Yb groups contributed decisively.
responses.response: I agree that breadth of opening support is information about robustness across lenses and not a measure of merit, and I have tried to rest my own case on the physical step that distinguishes lattice clocks. I differ on timing: I would not wait for the redefinition. The performance is reproduced by independent laboratories now, and waiting makes the prize depend on a metrology decision that follows other considerations such as the choice among clock species. I accept your point on the other groups, which I raised myself, and I think the answer is a citation that says invention and realization. Your remark on my own Higgs ranking in round 1 is also fair, and I have accepted that the credit rule there is unresolved. I should add that your circuit QED interest means you are well placed to say the 2025 discount is real, and I take that in the same spirit as your own disclosure.

responses.point: Mehlig moved the clocks to first but argues that B008 is arguably more far-reaching in science, and does not want a clean attribution to count for more than the science. He also asks whether the citation should centre on Katori's concept or on Ye's performance.
responses.response: I share the worry that clean credit must not substitute for scientific merit, and I have said that B006 and B008 are arguably higher in pure significance. Where I come out differently is that the lattice clock is more than a clean attribution: the shift from a single ion to a many-atom ensemble in a magic-wavelength lattice is a conceptual step, and it has opened tests of fundamental constants and of gravitational redshift at millimetre scale. On your question I would not choose between concept and performance. The citation should name the invention and its realization together, since the two names are exactly the idea and its demonstration. Dividing the prize into the concept for Katori and the performance for Ye would misdescribe both, since Katori also built the first strontium clocks and Ye's group contributed to systematic control. I would add that the third seat should stay empty and not be filled for the sake of a number.

responses.point: Kroll asks whether Ye's credit is for the lattice clock specifically or for a wider programme in combs, ultracold matter and many-body spectroscopy, which could blur the citation.
responses.response: This is the right question and I would answer it in the citation. Ye's credit for this prize should be for taking the lattice clock to its accuracy and stability limit, including the control of many-body and density shifts and the laser coherence needed. His earlier comb work is already recognised through the 2005 prize and should not be counted again, and I would exclude it explicitly from our reasoning. If the committee reads his contribution as the broader programme, the case becomes weaker, so I would keep the wording to the clock. I also note that you disclose time in Hall's laboratory. It is a background connection to the comb tradition and not a tie to Katori or Ye, and I would not treat it as disqualifying.

responses.point: Lindroth treats the timing as natural after combs in 2005 and ion control in 2012, regards recognition as neither premature nor a lifetime award, and notes that Ye's role is partly a continuation of a programme recognised in 2005.
responses.response: I agree on maturity and on the observation that Ye's role partly continues an honoured programme. That is why I want the citation tied to the lattice clock and its realization, and not to timekeeping in general. We differ slightly on how clean the attribution is: I still think it is the cleanest on the shortlist, but not clean in an absolute sense, because Lemonde and Takamoto and the PTB and NIST groups did essential work. In round 1 I wrote that we should be careful, and I stay with that. I also note your disclosure about ETH Zurich, the institution of Wallraff on B004. It is relevant only if B004 becomes a leading option, which it does not appear to be for me.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards lattice clocks as a distinct invention and not as an extension of the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. I think they are distinct but I cannot prove this from the supplied text.
Whether a two-name prize is fair to Lemonde, Takamoto, Lisdat and the Yb and ion-clock groups; I cannot verify detailed priority from the supplied material.
Whether the citation should include the 10^-18 level, and whether this strengthens or merely adds a metric that is later surpassed.
I rely on my general knowledge for the clock accuracy records and the sequence of independent confirmations and have not verified them.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile. My documented connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet, the Uppsala theory group) do not appear among the credited names of any shortlisted candidate. I have noted the disclosures of Johansson, Olsson, Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce; none affects my vote on B035, and I see no need for a recusal on my side.
